tasks.title: Null and undefined control-flow errors
tasks.scope: Detect missing null/undefined guards before property access, method calls, or array indexing that can cause runtime TypeErrors.
tasks.prompt: You are analyzing TypeScript code for null and undefined control-flow errors that cause runtime failures. Find logical errors where code accesses properties, calls methods, or indexes into collections without verifying the target is not null or undefined. Inspect changed hunks and trace data flow from sources (function parameters, object properties, array elements, API responses, configuration values) to sinks (property access with dot or bracket notation, method invocation, array indexing, destructuring). Check whether TypeScript strict null checks are enabled in tsconfig.json; if disabled, this is itself evidence of missing compile-time protection. For each potentially unsafe access, trace backward to confirm whether a type guard, explicit null check, optional chaining, nullish coalescing, or early return protects the access. When a guard exists, verify it covers all code paths and does not rely on incorrect type narrowing (such as truthiness checks that treat empty string or zero as null). When analyzing optional chaining or nullish coalescing, confirm the fallback behavior is correct for the use case; silent undefined propagation can hide bugs. Use public TypeScript narrowing documentation at https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html to understand current narrowing behavior for typeof, instanceof, in, and user-defined type guards. Do not assume library functions perform null checks unless their type signatures require non-nullable inputs. If repository context is missing (such as whether a function parameter can be null in practice despite a non-nullable type annotation), note this in the finding rationale but do not report it as a bug unless the code itself contains contradictory evidence (such as defensive null checks in some callers but not others). Report findings only when you have concrete evidence: the changed line contains an unsafe access, data-flow analysis shows a nullable source reaches that access, and no guard exists on all paths. Each finding must cite the changed line number, the nullable source, the unsafe operation, and the missing guard. Do not report findings for intentional non-null assertions (exclamation mark operator) unless surrounding code suggests the assertion is incorrect. Do not report style issues, missing comments, or broader architectural concerns.
evidenceRequirements: Changed line number containing the property access, method call, or array index
Data-flow trace showing the nullable or undefined source (parameter, property, return value, or expression)
Concrete evidence that no null/undefined guard exists on all paths to the unsafe operation
TypeScript strict null check configuration status from tsconfig.json or inline compiler directives
Reference to public TypeScript narrowing documentation when analyzing guard correctness
outOfScope: Style preferences for guard syntax (if vs optional chaining vs early return)
Nullable values that are intentionally propagated with correct optional chaining
Non-null assertions that are correct based on surrounding invariants
Missing null checks in unchanged code unless directly relevant to understanding a changed-line bug

tasks.title: Async and promise control-flow errors
tasks.scope: Detect unhandled promise rejections, missing await keywords, race conditions, and async initialization errors that cause silent failures or incorrect ordering.
tasks.prompt: You are analyzing TypeScript code for asynchronous control-flow errors that cause silent failures, incorrect ordering, or unhandled rejections. Find logical errors in async/await usage, promise chains, parallel execution, and async initialization. Inspect changed hunks for: (1) promises returned from functions but not awaited or caught by callers, (2) async functions whose rejections are not handled with try/catch or .catch(), (3) missing await keywords where sequential ordering is required, (4) race conditions from concurrent operations that assume ordering (such as parallel writes to shared state or concurrent file operations without locking), (5) async initialization in constructors or top-level code that can fail silently, (6) event-loop blocking operations (synchronous I/O, CPU-intensive loops) inside async functions. For each issue, trace the async operation to confirm whether a handler exists. Check whether the repository uses a global unhandled rejection handler or process-level event listeners; if present, note this as mitigation but still report missing local handlers when local recovery is needed. Use public Node.js async guidance at https://nodejs.org/en/docs/guides/dont-block-the-event-loop/ to understand event-loop blocking and async patterns. When analyzing promise chains, verify that .then() and .catch() are used correctly and that errors propagate to a final handler. When analyzing Promise.all or Promise.race, confirm error handling covers partial failures. If deployment environment is unknown, note in the finding rationale how serverless or edge environments might amplify the impact (such as cold-start failures or request timeouts). Do not assume frameworks provide automatic rejection handling unless their documentation explicitly guarantees it. Report findings only when you have concrete evidence: the changed line introduces or modifies an async operation, data-flow or control-flow analysis shows the operation can reject or block, and no appropriate handler or await exists. Each finding must cite the changed line number, the async operation, the missing handler or await, and the potential runtime impact (silent failure, incorrect ordering, timeout, or crash). Do not report style preferences for async syntax, missing comments, or architectural concerns about async boundaries.

Evidence that no try/catch, .catch(), or process-level handler covers the rejection

tasks.title: Input validation and sanitization errors
tasks.scope: Detect missing or incorrect validation of user-supplied data, environment variables, configuration, and external API responses that can cause injection, type coercion bugs, or runtime errors.
tasks.prompt: You are analyzing TypeScript code for input validation and sanitization errors. Find logical errors where untrusted or external data flows into security-sensitive or error-prone operations without validation. Inspect changed hunks for data flows from sources (HTTP request parameters, headers, body; command-line arguments; environment variables; configuration files; database query results; external API responses; file contents) to sinks (SQL queries, shell commands, file paths, eval or Function constructors, HTML rendering, regular expressions, JSON.parse, parseInt/parseFloat, array indexing, object property access with bracket notation). For each flow, check whether validation exists: type checks, format checks (regex, schema validation), range checks, allow-list checks, sanitization (escaping, encoding), or explicit error handling for parse failures. When validation exists, verify it is correct: check for type coercion bugs (such as == vs ===, truthy checks that accept unexpected values), incomplete escaping, regex denial-of-service patterns, or missing checks for edge cases (empty string, negative numbers, special characters, very large inputs). Use public OWASP input validation guidance at https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html to assess validation completeness for injection-sensitive sinks. Trace data flow across function boundaries; if a helper function performs validation, confirm the caller uses it for all inputs of that type. If a schema validation library (such as zod, joi, ajv) is used, confirm the schema matches the sink requirements and that validation errors are handled. If threat model or authentication boundaries are unknown, note in the finding rationale which inputs might be trusted in some deployments; still report missing validation unless the code contains evidence that the input source is always trusted (such as hardcoded values or results from a trusted internal API with documented contracts). Do not assume TypeScript types provide runtime validation; type annotations are compile-time only. Report findings only when you have concrete evidence: the changed line introduces or modifies a data flow from an untrusted source to a sensitive sink, and validation is missing or incorrect. Each finding must cite the changed line number, the untrusted source, the sensitive sink, the missing or incorrect validation, and the potential impact (injection, crash, incorrect behavior). Do not report style issues, missing comments, or architectural concerns about input handling.

tasks.title: Error handling and recovery logic errors
tasks.scope: Detect incorrect error handling that swallows errors, returns wrong error types, fails to clean up resources, or allows invalid state after errors.
tasks.prompt: You are analyzing TypeScript code for error handling and recovery logic errors. Find logical errors in try/catch blocks, error propagation, error type checking, resource cleanup, and state recovery after errors. Inspect changed hunks for: (1) empty catch blocks or catch blocks that log but do not propagate or recover, (2) incorrect error type checks (such as catching all errors but only handling specific types, or using string matching on error messages instead of error codes or types), (3) missing finally blocks or cleanup code for resources (file handles, database connections, timers, event listeners), (4) state mutations before error-prone operations without rollback or compensation, (5) re-throwing errors with lost context (such as throw new Error without wrapping the original error), (6) returning success values or default values from catch blocks when callers expect errors to propagate. For each issue, trace control flow to confirm whether the error can propagate correctly and whether resources are cleaned up on all paths (success, error, early return). Check whether the repository uses a standard error class hierarchy or error codes; if so, verify error handling respects those conventions. If the codebase uses a framework with automatic error boundaries (such as Express error middleware), confirm changed code integrates correctly with those boundaries. Trace error propagation across function boundaries; if a function catches and logs an error but does not re-throw or return an error value, confirm callers can detect the failure. For resource cleanup, check whether the repository uses RAII patterns, async cleanup hooks, or manual cleanup; verify the chosen pattern is used consistently. If deployment or framework context is missing, note in the finding rationale how missing error boundaries might affect impact; still report errors that prevent callers from detecting failures or that leak resources. Report findings only when you have concrete evidence: the changed line introduces or modifies error handling, control-flow analysis shows the error is swallowed or resources are not cleaned up, and the behavior contradicts reasonable caller expectations or framework contracts. Each finding must cite the changed line number, the error handling issue, the affected control-flow paths, and the potential impact (silent failure, resource leak, invalid state, lost error context). Do not report style preferences for error handling syntax, missing comments, or architectural concerns about error propagation strategies.

tasks.title: Type system misuse and unsound type assertions
tasks.scope: Detect use of unsafe type assertions, incorrect type narrowing, type system escape hatches (any, as, non-null assertions) that hide runtime type errors.
tasks.prompt: You are analyzing TypeScript code for type system misuse that hides runtime type errors. Find logical errors in type assertions, type guards, type casting, and use of TypeScript escape hatches (any, unknown, as, non-null assertions). Inspect changed hunks for: (1) type assertions (as, angle-bracket syntax) that are not justified by runtime evidence or control flow, (2) non-null assertions (exclamation mark operator) that assume a value is non-null without guards, (3) use of any type that disables type checking for values that flow into type-sensitive operations, (4) incorrect type guards that do not actually narrow types correctly (such as typeof checks that do not cover all union members, or user-defined type guards with incorrect return types), (5) type casting that widens types unsafely (such as casting a specific error type to unknown and losing type information), (6) reliance on TypeScript types for runtime validation without runtime checks. For each issue, trace data flow to confirm whether the asserted type matches runtime reality. Check whether the repository has a linting rule or convention that restricts type assertions; if so, verify the changed code complies. Use public TypeScript FAQ at https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/FAQ#common-bugs-that-arent-bugs to understand common type system pitfalls and unsound patterns. When analyzing type guards, verify the guard function checks all properties required to distinguish union members and that the return type is a valid type predicate. When analyzing any usage, trace the any-typed value to confirm it does not flow into operations that assume a specific type. If the repository uses strict TypeScript compiler options, check tsconfig.json to confirm; if strict mode is disabled, note this as evidence of reduced type safety but only report specific misuse in changed code. Do not assume type assertions are incorrect just because they use as syntax; report only when surrounding code or data flow contradicts the assertion. Report findings only when you have concrete evidence: the changed line contains a type assertion or escape hatch, data-flow or control-flow analysis shows the assertion is incorrect or unsafe, and the code lacks runtime checks to validate the assumption. Each finding must cite the changed line number, the type assertion or escape hatch, the data-flow evidence that contradicts the assertion, and the potential runtime impact (type error, incorrect behavior, crash). Do not report style preferences for type syntax, missing comments, or architectural concerns about type design.

tasks.title: State mutation and consistency errors
tasks.scope: Detect inconsistent state updates, mutation of shared state without synchronization, incorrect ordering of state changes, and stale closure references.
tasks.prompt: You are analyzing TypeScript code for state mutation and consistency errors. Find logical errors in object mutation, class property updates, shared state modification, and closure references that cause incorrect state, race conditions, or stale data. Inspect changed hunks for: (1) partial state updates that leave objects in inconsistent states (such as updating one property but not related properties, or updating derived state without recalculating it), (2) mutation of shared state (module-level variables, class static properties, singleton instances) without synchronization or locking, (3) incorrect ordering of state changes that violates invariants (such as setting a flag before the operation completes, or clearing a cache before writing new data), (4) stale closure references where a callback or event handler captures a variable value that later changes, (5) mutation of objects that are assumed to be immutable by other code (such as function parameters, cached objects, or objects returned from functions), (6) missing deep cloning when creating defensive copies. For each issue, trace state flow to confirm whether the mutation can cause observable inconsistency or race conditions. Check whether the repository uses immutability patterns (such as Object.freeze, readonly types, immutable libraries); if so, verify changed code respects those patterns. Check whether the repository uses state management libraries (such as Redux, MobX) with specific mutation rules; if so, verify changed code follows those rules. For shared state, confirm whether concurrent access is possible (such as multiple async operations, event handlers, or timers); if so, verify synchronization exists. For closures, trace variable references to confirm whether the captured value is stable or whether the closure should use a snapshot. If the repository architecture or concurrency model is unknown, note in the finding rationale how concurrent access might occur; still report inconsistent updates that violate obvious invariants. Report findings only when you have concrete evidence: the changed line mutates state, control-flow or data-flow analysis shows the mutation can cause inconsistency or staleness, and no synchronization or ordering constraint prevents the issue. Each finding must cite the changed line number, the state mutation, the inconsistency or race condition, and the potential impact (incorrect behavior, corrupted data, race condition). Do not report style preferences for immutability patterns, missing comments, or architectural concerns about state management design.

tasks.title: Resource lifecycle and cleanup errors
tasks.scope: Detect resource leaks, missing cleanup for file handles, timers, event listeners, database connections, and child processes.
tasks.prompt: You are analyzing TypeScript code for resource lifecycle and cleanup errors. Find logical errors in resource acquisition, usage, and cleanup that cause leaks, handle exhaustion, or zombie processes. Inspect changed hunks for: (1) file handles opened without close calls on all paths (success, error, early return), (2) timers (setTimeout, setInterval) started without clearTimeout or clearInterval, (3) event listeners added without removeEventListener or off calls, (4) database connections or HTTP clients opened without close or destroy calls, (5) child processes spawned without exit handlers or kill calls, (6) streams created without end, destroy, or error handlers, (7) AbortController signals created but not used to cancel pending operations, (8) missing cleanup in React useEffect or similar lifecycle hooks. For each issue, trace control flow to confirm whether cleanup exists on all paths, including error paths and early returns. Check whether the repository uses RAII patterns, automatic cleanup hooks (such as try/finally, AsyncDisposable, Symbol.dispose), or manual cleanup conventions; verify changed code follows those patterns. For event listeners and streams, confirm cleanup is idempotent (removing a listener multiple times is safe). For timers, confirm they are cleared before the component or module unloads. For child processes, confirm exit and error events are handled to prevent zombies. If framework lifecycle hooks are used (such as React useEffect, Angular ngOnDestroy), verify cleanup logic is returned or registered. If deployment or runtime environment is unknown, note in the finding rationale how long-lived processes (servers, daemons) vs short-lived processes (CLI scripts, serverless functions) affect leak impact; still report missing cleanup that can cause resource exhaustion. Report findings only when you have concrete evidence: the changed line acquires a resource, control-flow analysis shows cleanup is missing on some path, and the resource type requires explicit cleanup. Each finding must cite the changed line number, the resource type, the missing cleanup path, and the potential impact (leak, handle exhaustion, zombie process). Do not report style preferences for cleanup patterns, missing comments, or architectural concerns about resource management design.
